paragraphs: Learning useful representations without labels involves more than separating broad categories. Data can also contain finer distinctions and nested relationships that should remain visible in the learned representation. This paper argues that conventional contrastive learning often misses that structure because it treats alignment across the whole representation space too uniformly.

AMA-alignment introduces contrastive objectives that operate locally, alongside an adaptive strategy that works at multiple scales. Rather than giving every region the same treatment, it identifies areas where representations poorly reflect semantic relationships and directs refinement toward them. Working across scales lets the method address both broader organization and more detailed local relationships.

The additional machinery makes the model more complex, but the authors provide a convergence-rate guarantee comparable to standard smooth non-convex optimization. This concerns optimization behavior, rather than a claim that every run finds an ideal representation. Experiments across diverse benchmarks show preservation of hierarchical structure and improvements over existing contrastive methods on downstream tasks, supporting the value of explicitly modeling local relationships.
neurips-2025-adaptive-and-multi-scale-af.tldr: AMA-alignment adaptively refines local relationships at multiple scales to preserve hierarchy in representations learned without labels.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines learning across clients whose datasets remain decentralized. A central difficulty is that those datasets can differ substantially, so a single shared model may not fit every client well. Personalized federated learning addresses this by combining information learned globally with modeling adapted to each client's characteristics.

This paper investigates adaptive MMD measures as a way to constrain learned representations in personalized federated learning. These measures provide a distribution-comparison mechanism for handling differences between clients. The main investigation uses Ditto, a framework designed for heterogeneous distributed data, and studies whether theoretically supported, adaptive constraints improve its performance.

The reported results show significant improvements across multiple tasks, especially when clients differ strongly in their features. Additional experiments apply the measures to other personalization techniques and find similar benefits across several datasets. Together, these findings motivate choosing constraints according to the kind of heterogeneity a federated system encounters. The contribution is therefore both a concrete improvement to existing methods and evidence that representation constraints should reflect how client data differ.
neurips-2025-adaptive-latent-space-const.tldr: Adaptive distribution-based constraints improve personalized federated learning, particularly when clients have substantially different features.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares how mass is distributed across a space by accounting for movement between locations. This paper considers graph-based spaces where the two distributions can have different total masses. That matters when observations contain mass variation, noisy locations, or outliers. Existing transport approaches using flexible Orlicz geometry either require equal mass or become computationally complicated when extended.

The authors first develop Orlicz-EPT, an entropy partial transport formulation that incorporates Orlicz geometry, and establish a binary-search approach for solving it. They then use its dual formulation and the graph's structure to construct a regularized alternative called Orlicz-Sobolev transport, or OST. Its central computational advantage is that evaluation reduces to optimizing a function of one variable.

The paper derives geometric properties of OST and connections to other transport distances. Experiments find it several orders of magnitude faster than Orlicz-EPT. Applications to document classification and topological data analysis provide preliminary evidence of practical benefits. Those application results are exploratory support, while the computational simplification is the main methodological contribution.
neurips-2025-an-efficient-orlicz-sobolev.tldr: Orlicz-Sobolev transport compares unequal-mass measures on graphs through a one-variable optimization, with substantial reported speed advantages.

paragraphs: Learning physical dynamics is difficult when measurements cover only part of a system and arrive at irregular spatial locations. Methods tied to fixed spatial grids and time steps can struggle to represent continuous evolution from such observations. CoPS addresses this problem with a purely data-driven approach to modeling physics across space and time.

The method first combines observation values with their spatial information using a multiplicative filter network. It then constructs customized geometric grids and transfers features from the original observation locations onto those grids through message passing. This creates a structured representation from sparse, unstructured inputs without requiring the observations themselves to follow a fixed grid.

CoPS models temporal evolution through graph ordinary differential equations operating at multiple scales. A Markov-based neural correction module helps guide and constrain extrapolation over continuous time. The reported experiments show advances over existing state-of-the-art methods across various continuous space-time modeling scenarios. The approach's significance lies in connecting irregular observations to continuous dynamics through learned components, rather than making a fixed observation discretization the defining structure of the simulation.
neurips-2025-breaking-the-discretization.tldr: CoPS combines spatial feature mapping, multiscale graph dynamics, and neural correction to learn continuous physics from partial observations.

paragraphs: Storage activity offers a useful view of ransomware because the malware directly interacts with stored data. However, learning from those activity streams is difficult when labels identify only broad stretches of malicious behavior. CLEAR supplies labels for individual input/output commands, allowing researchers to distinguish ransomware activity from benign operations within a stream.

The dataset contains 1,045 TiB of traffic and malicious activity from 137 ransomware variants. The authors report that it exceeds other publicly accessible datasets by two orders of magnitude in traffic and one order in variant coverage. They also identify its command-by-command labeling as unique among those datasets. Auxiliary features accompany the traffic, with ablation studies showing that these features improve performance.

The detailed labels enable sequential models that reportedly improve data loss prevention by up to 82% over existing state-of-the-art models. They also support a recovery task that selectively reverses commands identified as ransomware while preserving benign activity. Finally, the paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating models against unseen ransomware variants, addressing whether detection extends beyond the malware represented during training.
neurips-2025-clear-command-level-annotat.tldr: CLEAR provides individually labeled storage commands for ransomware detection, selective recovery, and evaluation against unseen variants.

paragraphs: When auctions repeatedly sell multiple identical items, a bidder must learn how to bid against other participants. This paper compares that learning problem in uniform-price and discriminatory auctions, two formats used in electricity markets and treasury auctions. Its viewpoint is a single bidder facing stochastic competitors, with regret measuring the cost of learning over repeated rounds.

At the worst-case level, the two formats have similar learning difficulty. With full-information feedback, regret scales roughly as the square root of the number of rounds. With bandit feedback, which provides more limited information, it scales roughly as the number of rounds raised to two-thirds. These rates suppress logarithmic factors.

Looking beyond worst-case analysis exposes differences that the shared rates conceal. In certain settings, uniform-price auctions permit square-root regret while discriminatory auctions retain the slower two-thirds-power rate. The authors also identify a similar separation when other participants are symmetric and each demands one item. The result suggests that auction structure can affect learning speed even when broad worst-case guarantees make the formats appear equivalent.
neurips-2025-comparing-uniform-price-and.tldr: Uniform-price and discriminatory auctions share worst-case regret rates, but some settings allow faster learning in uniform-price auctions.

paragraphs: Generating outdoor 3D scenes requires both plausible geometry and meaningful semantic organization. This paper addresses the task of generating such scenes from abstract freehand sketches, together with the shortage of suitable annotated data. It introduces SketchSem3D, described as the first large-scale benchmark for this setting using sketches and satellite-image annotations produced through pseudo-labeling.

The benchmark contains sketch-based versions of SemanticKITTI and KITTI-360. Each brings together LiDAR voxels, corresponding sketches, and annotated satellite images, supporting standardized evaluation across different data sources. Alongside the benchmark, the authors introduce Cylinder Mamba Diffusion, or CymbaDiff, to improve the spatial coherence of generated outdoor environments.

CymbaDiff organizes spatial processing to capture continuity around cylindrical structure and relationships across vertical levels. Its design aims to retain both nearby physical relationships and context spanning the scene. Experiments on SketchSem3D report better semantic consistency, spatial realism, and generalization across datasets. The combined contribution is an evaluation resource and a generation method whose structure explicitly reflects the spatial relationships that coherent outdoor scenes need.
neurips-2025-cymbadiff-structured-spatia.tldr: CymbaDiff uses structured spatial diffusion for coherent sketch-guided 3D outdoor scenes, alongside the new SketchSem3D benchmark.

paragraphs: Reward curves show whether a reinforcement learning agent improves, but reveal much less about how it behaves. This paper studies agents using methods inspired by neuroscience and the study of animal behavior. Its environment, ForageWorld, combines partial observability, scattered resource patches that become depleted, predator threats, and large spaces in which agents must forage.

The researchers examine behavior alongside internal neural activity to investigate strategy, memory, and planning. They find that model-free agents built with recurrent neural networks can develop structured behavior resembling planning through their internal dynamics. These agents do so without explicit memory modules or world models. The finding concerns emergent planning-like behavior, rather than establishing that every model-free agent plans.

Joint analysis reveals patterns in learning and representation that reward comparisons alone would miss. The authors organize their tools into a reusable framework connecting behavioral and representational features with diagnostic methods. This makes the contribution broader than a new environment: it offers a way to investigate increasingly complex agents and behaviors that may be difficult to characterize through reward alone.
neurips-2025-deep-rl-needs-deep-behavior.tldr: Behavioral and neural analysis reveals that recurrent model-free agents can develop planning-like foraging strategies without explicit world models.

paragraphs: Video generators learn relationships across changing appearances, positions, and time. This paper asks whether knowledge acquired for that richer task can help with controlled image generation. DRA-Ctrl provides a method for transferring a trained video generator into image tasks, making use of its ability to model long-range context and broad attention relationships.

The transfer must bridge a mismatch: video frames form a continuous sequence, while controlled image generation works with separate image outputs. DRA-Ctrl introduces a mixup-based transition strategy to smooth that adaptation. It also changes the attention structure through a tailored mask, intended to align textual instructions more closely with controls applied at the image level.

Experiments cover several image-generation tasks, including subject-driven generation and generation conditioned on spatial information. In these evaluations, the adapted video models outperform models trained directly on images. The findings support reusing expensive video generators for a wider range of visual tasks. They also motivate future unified visual generators, while the demonstrated contribution is the transfer and adaptation of video-model capabilities to controlled image synthesis.
neurips-2025-dimension-reduction-attack-.tldr: DRA-Ctrl adapts trained video generators to controlled image synthesis, outperforming directly image-trained models in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: End-to-end driving systems predict future trajectories directly from perception inputs. Training them to imitate people can produce trajectories that look human-like without adequately distinguishing unsafe choices. This paper also identifies a weakness in approaches that predict separate rule-based scores: their supervision can remain disconnected from the optimization of the driving policy itself.

DriveDPO brings imitation and safety information into policy learning. It first combines similarity to human behavior with rule-based safety scores to distill a unified policy distribution. This gives the optimization process a joint signal about desirable trajectories. It then applies an iterative direct preference optimization stage, aligning the policy with preferences expressed over entire trajectories.

On NAVSIM, the authors report a new state-of-the-art PDMS of 90.0. Qualitative examples from challenging scenarios also show safer and more reliable driving behavior. These findings support integrating safety-based preferences directly into trajectory selection and policy training. The evidence consists of benchmark performance and observed example behaviors; the method's central contribution is making safety information part of what the policy is optimized to prefer.
neurips-2025-drivedpo-policy-learning-vi.tldr: DriveDPO combines human imitation and rule-based safety preferences in policy optimization, achieving a reported NAVSIM PDMS of 90.0.

paragraphs: Visual navigation models must turn what a robot sees into useful movement decisions. Foundation models with transformer decoders can make this computationally expensive, creating difficulties for deployment on edge devices. DynaNav addresses that cost by adapting which features and layers it uses according to the complexity of the scene.

A trainable hard feature selector chooses a subset of features for sparse computation. This is intended to improve efficiency while making feature selection more interpretable. The same selection process is integrated with an early-exit mechanism, allowing computation to end before all layers are used. Bayesian optimization determines the exit thresholds that govern this decision.

The authors evaluate DynaNav on datasets based on real-world observations and in simulated environments. Relative to ViNT, they report a 2.6-fold reduction in FLOPs, 42.3% lower inference time, and 32.8% lower memory use, alongside better navigation performance across four public datasets. The results support adapting computation to scene requirements as a practical way to reduce several resource costs while retaining strong navigation behavior.
neurips-2025-dynanav-dynamic-feature-and.tldr: DynaNav dynamically selects features and processing depth to reduce navigation computation, latency, and memory while improving reported performance.

paragraphs: A model serving several tasks must balance their competing objectives. This paper focuses on finding a desired compromise near the Pareto front, where improving one objective entails sacrificing another. EXTRA explores connections between model solutions to locate useful tradeoffs, rather than attempting to learn a representation of the entire front.

The approach builds on mode connectivity, which studies low-loss paths through model parameter space. Such paths do not automatically cover useful tradeoffs or follow user preferences. EXTRA uses non-uniform rational B-splines to make the paths more flexible than commonly used Bézier curves. It adds an order-aware objective to organize exploration of task losses and groups tasks to improve scalability when many tasks are involved.

Experiments on major multi-task learning datasets report that EXTRA identifies desired Pareto-front points and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The method is also evaluated as an addition to mainstream multi-task learning approaches. Its significance is a practical way to search among compromises using flexible paths between solutions, making preference-directed exploration a central part of the procedure.
neurips-2025-exploring-tradeoffs-through.tldr: EXTRA uses flexible paths between model solutions to efficiently explore multi-task tradeoffs and find a preferred compromise.

paragraphs: Multimodal models increasingly combine visual understanding with image generation. Many use autoregressive prediction, whose sequential ordering constrains how context is incorporated and how images are generated. FUDOKI explores a unified model based entirely on discrete flow matching, providing an alternative way to perform both kinds of task.

Its generation process follows probability paths defined through a metric and kinetic-optimal velocities. This goes beyond a corruption process based only on masking, supporting repeated refinement, self-correction, and richer use of context in both directions. To reduce the cost of training a new model from the beginning, the authors initialize from pretrained autoregressive multimodal models and adaptively transition them to discrete flow matching.

Experiments show performance comparable to state-of-the-art autoregressive multimodal models on visual understanding and image generation. Applying test-time scaling also produces significant gains. These results establish discrete flow matching as a competitive basis for unified multimodal modeling in the reported evaluations. The authors see the gains as motivation for future reinforcement-learning improvements, rather than reporting those future improvements as an achieved result.
neurips-2025-fudoki-discrete-flow-based-.tldr: FUDOKI unifies visual understanding and image generation through discrete flow matching, with competitive performance and gains from test-time scaling.

paragraphs: Long-context language models must manage the cost of attention and the memory used to retain keys and values. Compressing this cache can help, but many methods handle keys and values in the same way. This paper argues that such uniform treatment overlooks an important empirical difference between the two kinds of cached information.

The authors find that adjacent keys receive similar attention weights, while adjacent values have distinct distributions. AsymKV uses that asymmetry to design separate compression strategies. It merges keys according to their local similarity and applies a value-compression method with a mathematical losslessness guarantee. The framework requires no training. The stated losslessness result belongs specifically to value compression, rather than establishing that the entire compression pipeline leaves outputs unchanged.

Across several tasks and base models, experiments report consistent improvements over existing long-context methods. On LLaMA3.1-8B, AsymKV obtains a LongBench average of 43.95, compared with 38.89 for H2O. The findings support tailoring cache compression to the different roles and observed properties of keys and values.
neurips-2025-homogeneous-keys-heterogene.tldr: AsymKV combines similarity-based key merging with provably lossless value compression to improve reported long-context performance without training.

paragraphs: Cooperative bandit learning asks how agents can share observations while learning which actions yield the best rewards. This paper studies agents connected by any connected communication graph. Its focus is the regret experienced by each individual agent, so the guarantee describes personal learning costs rather than only the group's combined performance.

For a variant of Cooperative Successive Elimination, the authors bound individual regret by O(R/m + A² + A√log T). Here R is the optimal single-agent regret expression, m is the number of agents, A is the number of actions, and T is the time horizon. The leading R/m term captures a benefit from cooperation, while the remaining terms represent additional costs. A nearly matching lower bound supports the strength of this guarantee.

Crucially, the bound does not depend on the graph's diameter, a first for individual regret in this setting according to the authors. It remains valid with logarithmic-size messages. A separate result restricts communication to logarithmically many rounds and obtains O(R/m + A log T), clarifying how learning guarantees interact with communication constraints.
neurips-2025-individual-regret-in-cooper.tldr: A cooperative bandit algorithm achieves individual regret guarantees independent of communication-graph diameter, including under communication restrictions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate probabilities over a finite set of symbols from independent samples, measuring error with KL divergence. It first constructs private estimators with optimal worst-case performance. However, a worst-case guarantee can conceal how an estimator behaves on particular distributions, and simple estimators with that guarantee can perform poorly on real data.

The authors therefore use instance-optimality: an estimator's error on a distribution is compared with the best achievable error over a small neighborhood of that distribution. Under natural definitions of these neighborhoods, they develop algorithms that match this local benchmark up to constant factors. They obtain results both with and without differential privacy constraints.

The estimators build on variants of the Good-Turing approach, including private versions. The lower-bound analysis uses additive local neighborhoods to capture the difficulty of KL estimation more precisely than neighborhoods used in prior work. The contribution gives a finer account of statistical difficulty: an algorithm can be evaluated against what is locally achievable for the distribution at hand, alongside its broad worst-case guarantee.
neurips-2025-instance-optimality-for-pri.tldr: Good-Turing-based estimators achieve locally instance-optimal KL error up to constant factors, with and without differential privacy.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts models offer an efficient route to scaling language models, but their deployment depends on both computing and memory resources. A system's cost, accuracy, and performance are therefore connected. MoE-CAP introduces a benchmark intended to make these relationships visible when comparing hardware platforms and deployment choices.

The authors' analysis finds that current hardware makes it difficult to optimize all three dimensions together. Systems typically favor two while sacrificing the third, a pattern they call the MoE-CAP trade-off. A CAP Radar Diagram presents these competing outcomes visually, helping comparisons account for more than a single measure of speed or accuracy.

The benchmark also introduces Sparse Memory Bandwidth Utilization and Sparse Model FLOPS Utilization. These metrics account for sparsity when evaluating memory and computational resource use. Together, the visualization and metrics aim to support more faithful assessments of mixture-of-experts systems across different settings. The reported trade-off describes a practical pattern on current hardware, rather than a universal impossibility of improving cost, accuracy, and performance simultaneously.
neurips-2025-moe-cap-benchmarking-cost-a.tldr: MoE-CAP benchmarks the coupled cost, accuracy, and performance tradeoffs of sparse mixture-of-experts deployments using sparsity-aware metrics.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a deployed model using incoming data without labels, helping it respond when those data differ from its training distribution. Yet adaptation can leave performance low enough that continued deployment is inappropriate. This paper addresses how to recognize those cases, rather than assuming that ongoing updates keep the model sufficiently reliable.

The authors pair adaptation with statistical risk monitoring that tracks predictive performance and signals when predefined criteria are violated. They extend monitoring methods built on sequential tests and confidence sequences, tools for assessing evidence as observations arrive. The challenge is to accommodate both a changing model and the absence of test labels for directly measuring the performance quantities of interest.

The resulting framework makes rigorous statistical monitoring applicable to test-time adaptation. The authors demonstrate its use across a representative collection of adaptation methods, datasets, and distribution shifts. This separates two deployment functions: adaptation tries to maintain useful predictions, while monitoring checks whether performance still meets the chosen requirements and can indicate when taking the model offline for retraining is warranted.
neurips-2025-monitoring-risks-in-test-ti.tldr: The paper extends statistical risk monitoring to detect performance failures in models adapting to unlabeled test data.

paragraphs: A video may contain several actions involving different objects at the same time. Representing all of them with one unified feature description can make their interactions difficult to distinguish. ProDA addresses this by constructing representations targeted to specified actions within a complex scene, making action separation part of the recognition process.

The framework uses spatio-temporal scene graphs to represent relationships across space and time. A Dynamic Prompt Module guides a Graph Parsing Neural Network toward an action-specific representation. The authors also adapt that network for video, allowing it to combine information with dynamic weights. These components provide a mechanism for changing which scene information contributes to the representation of a particular action.

Experiments on Charades and SportsHHI, two datasets involving complex video actions, demonstrate effectiveness against state-of-the-art methods. The findings support using prompts to guide how relational video information is assembled, especially when multiple actions share a scene. The contribution centers on making representations responsive to the action being considered, rather than asking one shared representation to describe every interaction equally.
neurips-2025-prompt-guided-disentangled-.tldr: ProDA uses prompts and spatio-temporal scene graphs to build action-specific representations for recognizing actions in complex videos.

paragraphs: Transformer-based imitation learning often converts actions into discrete codes before learning to generate them sequentially. The paper argues that this quantization disrupts the continuous structure of the action space and can constrain the generative model. Its central question is whether an autoregressive policy can work directly with continuous actions while retaining strong task performance.

The proposed method uses Generative Infinite-Vocabulary Transformers as a continuous policy parametrization. This removes the initial conversion into a finite set of action codes and simplifies the imitation-learning pipeline. The important distinction is between generating sequentially and generating discrete symbols: the approach retains autoregressive generation while changing the kind of action representation the model predicts.

On a variety of popular simulated robotics tasks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance. They also study sampling algorithms used during policy rollouts and obtain further improvements. These results indicate that both the continuous representation and the procedure for sampling actions matter to the resulting policy. The empirical support concerns simulated robotics, where the simpler quantization-free pipeline achieves strong reported results.
neurips-2025-quantization-free-autoregre.tldr: A continuous autoregressive action policy removes quantization and achieves state-of-the-art results on reported simulated robotics tasks.

paragraphs: Discrete flow models can generate high-quality discrete data, but typically require many decoding steps. This paper connects that cost to a factorization approximation used to handle high-dimensional data. The authors measure its error with conditional total correlation, a quantity describing dependencies left over under the factorization, and show that the error depends on the source-to-target coupling.

ReDi changes that coupling through an iterative rectification procedure. The aim is to make the relationship between source and target distributions easier for the factorized model to capture. The authors prove that each rectification step monotonically decreases conditional total correlation and establish convergence. This is a guarantee about the analyzed error quantity, giving a theoretical basis for the procedure.

Experiments show substantial reductions in conditional total correlation and support generation with fewer steps. The rectified couplings also work well for training one-step image-generation models. The contribution links a measurable approximation error to a concrete way of changing training relationships, offering a theoretically grounded route toward faster generation rather than relying only on reducing decoding steps directly.
neurips-2025-redi-rectified-discrete-flo.tldr: ReDi progressively reduces discrete-flow factorization error by rectifying source-target couplings, enabling effective few-step and one-step generation.

paragraphs: Adapting a large language model requires balancing trainable parameter count against flexibility. Low-rank adaptation offers efficiency but can restrict the forms an update can take. Mixture-of-experts designs offer greater capacity while introducing additional parameters that may be underused. S'MoRE combines these ideas through a structured collection of reusable low-rank components.

The method decomposes expert weights hierarchically into residuals of different orders, connected across multiple layers. Tokens are routed through subtrees of these residuals, assembling expert behavior from a relatively small number of low-rank matrices. This allows many expert configurations to be represented through combinations of shared components. The propagation between residual layers is formulated as a special graph neural network.

Under similar parameter budgets, the authors prove an exponential-order improvement in structural flexibility over traditional mixture-of-experts or mixtures of LoRA. That result concerns available structure, rather than an exponential improvement in task accuracy. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations also support superior fine-tuning performance, making structured reuse of low-rank residuals the central mechanism for efficient adaptation.
neurips-2025-s-more-structural-mixture-o.tldr: S'MoRE assembles many expert configurations from hierarchical low-rank residuals, improving structural flexibility and reported fine-tuning performance.

paragraphs: Sampling from a complicated distribution is difficult when its density is known only up to a normalization constant. Score-based approaches often require a learned score approximation or costly nested Markov chain Monte Carlo calculations. This paper proposes estimating intermediate scores along a diffusion path through stochastic averaging, avoiding both training and inner-loop MCMC.

The framework couples slow and fast stochastic differential equations, using the averaging behavior of the fast dynamics to estimate information needed along the path. It yields two algorithms: MultALMC, based on multiscale annealed Langevin dynamics, and MultCDiff, based on controlled diffusions for a reverse-time Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Both overdamped and underdamped variants are considered, with convergence guarantees to the desired diffusion path.

The authors also adapt the framework to heavy-tailed targets using Student's t noise and specially designed fast dynamics. Tests on synthetic and real-world problems include multimodal and high-dimensional distributions. The reported methods are competitive with existing samplers in accuracy and efficiency, supporting multiscale averaging as an alternative when learned models or nested sampling would be undesirable.
neurips-2025-sampling-by-averaging-a-mul.tldr: Multiscale stochastic averaging estimates diffusion-path scores without training or inner-loop MCMC, yielding competitive sampling methods.

paragraphs: An object's appearance can change dramatically while it remains part of the same unfolding event. Cutting an apple into pieces illustrates why following appearance alone may lose the object of interest. This paper introduces Track Any State, a task that combines tracking through transformations with detecting and describing the associated state changes.

The authors provide the VOST-TAS benchmark and a zero-shot system called TubeletGraph. The system first searches for tracks that may have been overlooked after a transformation. It decides whether to integrate them using semantic relationships and proximity. It then reasons about the added tracks and constructs a state graph recording how the observed object states change over time.

TubeletGraph achieves state-of-the-art tracking performance under transformations in the reported evaluation. It also demonstrates deeper transformation understanding and promising abilities in temporal grounding and semantic reasoning. The contribution extends tracking beyond maintaining a location: the recovered tracks are linked into an account of what changed and when, connecting continuity of observation with an explanation of evolving object states.
neurips-2025-tracking-and-understanding-.tldr: TubeletGraph recovers objects after transformations and builds state graphs describing their changes, alongside a new tracking benchmark.

paragraphs: Semantic scene completion reconstructs both the 3D shape and semantic categories of an environment. Treating it as independent classification of small spatial cells, or voxels, can miss object-level structure and blur distinctions between neighboring objects. VoxDet reformulates the task around dense detection, using information about object boundaries to guide semantic predictions.

The first component, VoxNT, converts existing voxel class labels into instance-level offset labels without training. VoxDet then separates feature processing into offset regression and semantic prediction. Its spatially decoupled encoder creates task-specific feature volumes, while a dense predictor estimates distances from voxels to object boundaries in six directions. These offsets guide the classification branch in aggregating information at the object-instance level.

This design makes boundary relationships part of the scene-completion process, helping organize predictions around objects rather than only individual cells. The method supports both camera and LiDAR inputs and reports state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks. On the SemanticKITTI test set, it achieves 63.0 IoU and is reported as ranking first on the online leaderboard.
neurips-2025-voxdet-rethinking-3d-semant.tldr: VoxDet uses object-boundary offsets derived from voxel labels to make 3D semantic scene completion instance-aware.
